content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are the immature seeds of the pea plant (Pisum sativum), which grow in pods. They taste mildly sweet and are tender and slightly starchy. Peas are eaten fresh, frozen, or canned and added to soups, side dishes, stews, pasta, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas are legumes, and the edible "peas" are the seeds inside the pod.
Gregor Mendel's experiments with pea plants laid the foundation of modern genetics.
Frozen peas are usually frozen soon after harvest, so they keep their flavor and nutrients well.
Snap peas and snow peas are eaten together with their pods.
Peas have been grown for thousands of years and remain one of the most popular vegetable crops.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Green peas provide more protein than many other vegetables and can be part of a plant-based diet.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full for longer.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K plays a role in blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C and folate
items.content: Peas provide vitamin C and folate, which are important for the immune system and cell formation.

items.title: Contains lutein and zeaxanthin
items.content: These carotenoids are antioxidants linked to eye health.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Peas contain carbohydrates that may cause gas and bloating in some people.

items.title: Salt in canned peas
items.content: Canned peas may contain added salt; rinsing them before use can help.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Peas are legumes, and allergies are possible, including cross-reactions with other legumes.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole peas can be a choking risk for small children, so it is best to mash them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh young peas can be eaten raw or briefly steamed or boiled for 2–3 minutes to keep their color and sweetness. Frozen peas can be added straight from the freezer to soups, rice, pasta, and purees. Avoid overcooking, which makes them mushy and bland.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh peas in their pods in the refrigerator and use them within two to three days, as their sugars quickly turn to starch. Keep frozen peas in the freezer in a sealed package. Store canned peas in a cool place, and after opening, transfer them to a covered container in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Knish is a traditional Jewish pastry, usually made from a yeasted dough and filled with meat, potatoes, cabbage, or cheese. The dough is soft, slightly crisp on the outside and tender inside, while the filling gives the snack a rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Knish originated in Eastern Europe in the 19th century and quickly became popular among Jewish communities.
There are many filling variations: beef, chicken, potato, sauerkraut, cheese, and even sweet versions with fruit.
Traditionally knishes are sold at street stalls and Jewish holidays, especially Hanukkah.
In the United States knishes are often served as a fast‑food style snack in Jewish delicatessens.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Meat or cheese fillings provide a substantial amount of protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meaty fillings are rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough and meat fillings contain B1, B2, B3, and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: Yeasted dough supplies quick‑acting carbohydrates useful during physical activity.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Knish is calorie‑dense due to dough and fatty fillings, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Salty fillings and added seasonings can raise sodium intake, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat‑based dough contains gluten, making knish unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked meat fillings may harbor pathogenic bacteria; ensure the knish is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Knish is typically served hot, cut in half. It can be eaten as a snack on its own, added to a salad, or served as part of a appetizer spread. For a lighter taste, drizzle a little sour cream or tomato sauce over it.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store knish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Before reheating, make sure the filling reaches an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato french fries are sliced potatoes that are blanched, flash‑frozen, and ready for frying. When cooked they become crispy with a golden exterior and a soft interior. The product is widely used in fast‑food restaurants and home kitchens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial french fries appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
Freezing preserves the flavor and texture of the fries for several months.
Different countries serve fries with a variety of sauces: ketchup, mayonnaise, tartar sauce, etc.
There are “shoestring” and “steak‑cut” cuts, each offering distinct culinary qualities.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, though much of it is lost during frying.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Potatoes provide fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Frying adds significant calories and saturated fats to the fries.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature cooking can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound; avoid over‑cooking.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Fries are often salted, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Heat oil to 175‑180 °C (350‑356 °F). Add frozen strips and fry for 3‑5 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain on paper towels, season with salt to taste, and serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen french fries in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. After opening, use within 3‑4 months. Do not thaw before frying.

content.title: About
content.content: Sauerkraut is a fermented product made from fresh white cabbage, salt, and sometimes spices. During fermentation, lactic‑acid bacteria convert the cabbage sugars into lactic acid, giving it a characteristic sour taste and extending its shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sauerkraut is a traditional dish in many Eastern and Central European countries.
Fermentation creates probiotic cultures that are beneficial for gut health.
The acidic environment helps preserve vitamin C, which is usually lost during cooking.
In Russia, sauerkraut is commonly used in soups like shchi and borscht, as well as a side dish.
The most famous variety is German sauerkraut, often flavored with caraway seeds and apples.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Fermentation produces live Lactobacillus bacteria that support a healthy intestinal microbiome.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Sauerkraut retains a high level of vitamin C, which helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Rich in dietary fiber, it aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low Calorie
items.content: One cup of sauerkraut contains about 20 calories, making it a great choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides potassium, magnesium, and iron, important for heart function and blood formation.

items.title: High Sodium Content
items.content: Sauerkraut often contains a lot of salt, which can be an issue for people with hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial Fermentation
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of harmful bacteria and spoilage.

items.title: Gas and Bloating
items.content: For some individuals, fermentation may cause increased gas and abdominal discomfort.

items.title: Cabbage Allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergic reaction to cabbage or its fermented forms can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauerkraut can be eaten on its own as a snack, added to soups, stews, salads, sandwiches, or used as a side dish for meat and fish. It is often rinsed before serving to reduce excess salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sauerkraut in the refrigerator in an airtight container. When kept properly, it stays fresh for 2–3 weeks. Discard if you notice mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp chips are crunchy snacks made from rice or potato flour and flavored with powdered dried shrimp. They have a light marine taste, a hint of salt, and a distinctive seafood aroma. The chips are typically deep‑fried until golden and crisp.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp chips are especially popular in Japan, China, and Southeast Asia, where they are often served with beer.
Natural paprika or beet extract is sometimes added to give them a bright pink hue.
The dried shrimp used for seasoning are heat‑treated, preserving flavor while ensuring safety.
Compared with traditional potato chips, shrimp chips usually contain less fat but more protein thanks to the seafood component.
In some markets they are called “shrimp crackers” or “prawn chips.”

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The dried shrimp in the chips provide a modest amount of easily digestible marine protein.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Unlike sweet snacks, shrimp chips contain virtually no sugar.

items.title: Rich in iodine
items.content: Shrimp is a natural source of iodine, important for thyroid function.

items.title: Contains omega‑3
items.content: Small amounts of omega‑3 fatty acids may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They provide vitamin B12 and niacin, which help with metabolism.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp chips can trigger allergic reactions in people sensitive to crustaceans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties are high in salt, so those with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Deep‑frying can create trans fats; choose products labeled “no trans fats” when possible.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although lighter than potato chips, they are still calorie‑dense – moderation is key.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Shrimp chips are perfect as a standalone snack, with beer, or as a side to Asian dishes. They can be tossed with extra seasonings such as chili, lime, or dried garlic for added flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the chips in an airtight bag in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to maintain crunch and aroma.
